lesson.title: When forces balance

lead.text: To put numbers on the rope we need a unit. A push or a pull on an object is called a force, and forces are measured in newtons, written N. One newton is roughly the pull of gravity on a small apple, so the pull of a tug-of-war team, a few hundred newtons, is a strong one. Suppose the left team pulls with 400 N and the right team with 350 N.

A force has a direction as well as a size, and we draw it as an arrow that points the way it pulls. The two teams' arrows lie along the same rope and point opposite ways, so they work against each other. The smaller pull takes away part of the larger one, and what is left over decides which way the flag slides. The left team wins, and the size of its lead is the amount the two pulls leave over.
Think of the rope as the object. Two arrows act on it, one in each direction.

reveal.text: The smaller pull cancels part of the larger one, so the lead is 400 − 350 newtons.

lead.text: The leftover in the tug of war has a name. It is the net force on the rope, the combined effect of every force acting on it. To find the net force on any object, first decide which object you mean, because only the forces acting on that object count. Then choose a direction to count as positive. Say it is right. A force pointing right gets a plus sign and a force pointing left gets a minus sign.

For the rope, the right team gives +350 N and the left team gives −400 N. Added together they make −50 N, which is the answer to the last question with a direction attached. The size, 50 N, says how much is left over, and the minus sign says the leftover points left, so the flag slides towards the stronger team.

afterFigure.text: The same rule works for any number of forces. Give each force its sign and add them all. A plus sign on the result means the net force points the way you chose as positive, and a minus sign means it points the other way.

lead.text: Two horizontal forces act on a cart. One points right and one points left. Right is positive.

reveal.text: You gave the leftward force a minus sign and added: 14 − 6. The sum points right, so it is positive.

steps.headline: A sled has forces of 12 N right, 7 N left and 3 N left. Find the net force.

workedSteps.text: Give each force its sign, rightward positive.
The result is small and positive, so the sled's net push is slightly to the right.

steps.headline: A resting cart has 9 N right and 9 N left on it. What is the net force?

workedSteps.text: The rightward force counts as positive.
The leftward force counts as negative.

steps.headline: What a net force of zero does

lead.text: The last example had a cart with 9 N pulling one way and 9 N pulling the other, and the sum came to zero. When the net force on an object is zero we say the forces on it are balanced. Their effects cancel, and the object behaves as if nothing were acting on it.

For an object at rest that is easy to accept, since a book on a table stays where it is. The surprise is what happens to something already moving. A cart rolling at 5 m/s with balanced forces on it carries on at 5 m/s, in the same direction, for as long as the forces stay balanced. Nothing has to keep pushing it.

afterFigure.text: Everyday life seems to say otherwise, because a ball rolling over grass slows and stops. The reason is a second force that we left out, friction, the rubbing of the grass against the ball. The forces on the ball are no longer balanced, which is why its velocity changes. A puck on smooth ice has very little friction and slides a long way at nearly the same speed. The rule that balanced forces leave the velocity unchanged is called Newton's first law of motion.

cases.label: Rolling at 5 m/s, 12 N each way

lead.text: A cart rolls right at 3 m/s. The forces on it add up to zero.

reveal.text: Zero net force means no change in velocity, so the cart keeps its 3 m/s. It needs no push to keep going.

steps.headline: A force that points against the motion

lead.text: Now unbalance the forces. A cart is rolling to the right, and the net force on it points left. A force says nothing about where an object is going. It says how the velocity changes. A leftward net force pushes the velocity towards the left, so the cart's rightward velocity shrinks. The cart slows, stops for an instant and, if the force keeps acting, starts to move left.

The direction of the net force and the direction of the motion are separate things. When they agree, the object speeds up. When they point opposite ways, it slows down. That matches what you found about speeding up and slowing down in the lesson on changing velocity, and it adds where the change comes from: a net force.
A cart rolls right, but the bigger force on it points left.

reveal.text: The net force points left while the cart still moves right. The force changes the velocity; it does not show where the cart is going.

lesson.orientation: Add signed forces and distinguish balanced forces from being at rest.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two teams take hold of a rope. One team pulls to the left as hard as it can and the other pulls to the right. A flag tied to the middle of the rope hangs over a line painted on the grass, and everyone watches the flag. For a while it hardly moves. Then, slowly, it begins to slide towards one side.

In the last lesson the stone had only one pull on it, from gravity, so we only had to ask how that single pull changed its motion. Almost everything else around you has several pushes and pulls on it at once. A book on a table and a swimmer in a pool both do, and what each one does depends on how its pushes and pulls add up.

This lesson follows the rope. We put numbers on the pulls and add them, then find out what an object does when they cancel exactly, which is less obvious than it sounds. We finish with a cart that is rolling one way while the bigger pull on it points the other way.

intro.promise: By the end you'll add up the pushes and pulls on an object, and say what happens to its velocity when they cancel.

recap.keyIdea: The net force is the signed sum of the forces on one object. When it is zero, the velocity does not change.

blocks.text: You found that a 400 N pull and a 350 N pull leave 50 N over, and that a cart with balanced forces keeps rolling at 3 m/s. You also met a net force of −12 N acting on a cart that was still moving to the right.

recap.nextHook: A net force of zero leaves the velocity alone. Next we find out how much the velocity changes when the net force is not zero.

questions.prompt: Two horizontal forces act on a cart: 14 N right and 6 N left. With right positive, find the net force in newtons.
hints: Give opposite directions opposite signs.
Add the signed forces on the same cart.
Calculate 14 − 6.
questions.onCorrect: +8 N. Net force is the signed sum of the forces on one object, with opposite directions given opposite signs.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes. The leftward force pulls against the rightward one, so subtract.
The size is right, but the larger force points right. The net force is positive.

questions.prompt: A cart is rolling right at 3 m/s on a track with no friction, and the net force on it stays zero. What happens next?
hints: Balanced forces imply no change in velocity.

acceptedIdeas: It continues at 3 m/s to the right
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero net force leaves the velocity unchanged.

choices.label: It continues at 3 m/s to the right

questions.onCorrect: It keeps going at 3 m/s to the right. Zero net force means no change in velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: Stopping would need a net force opposing the motion. Balanced forces leave the velocity as it is.
Gaining speed would need a net force in the direction of motion. Here it is zero.

questions.prompt: A resting cart has 9 N rightward and 9 N leftward horizontal forces. Find its horizontal net force in newtons.
hints: Compare the two force magnitudes.
Use opposite signs for opposite directions.
Calculate 9 − 9.
questions.onCorrect: 0 N. Equal forces in opposite directions add to zero: balanced forces.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sizes. The forces point opposite ways, so one takes the other away.
That is one of the two forces. Add both with their signs.

questions.prompt: A cart moving right experiences 8 N right and 20 N left. With right positive, find the net force in newtons.
hints: Separate the velocity direction from the force sum.
The leftward force enters with a minus sign.
Calculate 8 − 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 20 = −12 N. The net force is leftward even while the cart moves right.

questions.onCorrect: −12 N. The net force points left even though the cart moves right: it slows the cart down.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the larger force points left. The net force is negative.
That adds the sizes. The two forces point opposite ways, so subtract.

questions.prompt: Forces of 7 N and 11 N act rightward on a crate; a 5 N force acts leftward. Find the net force in newtons with right positive.
hints: Group the forces pointing in the same direction.
Add the two rightward forces, then subtract the leftward force.
Calculate 7 + 11 − 5.
questions.onCorrect: +13 N. Add the rightward forces, then take off the leftward one.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the rightward forces are larger. The net force is positive.
That adds all three as if they pointed the same way. The 5 N force points the other way.

questions.prompt: An object moves left at a constant velocity that is not zero. What is the net force on it?
hints: A continuing velocity does not require a continuing net push.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the net force is zero.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the forces on the object balance.

misconceptions.feedback: A net leftward force would make it accelerate leftward. Its velocity is not changing.
A net rightward force would slow it down. Its velocity is not changing.

questions.prompt: In a tug of war the left team pulls with 400 N and the right team pulls with 350 N. By how many newtons does the stronger pull win?
hints: Which pull is bigger?
The smaller pull cancels part of the larger one.
Take the 350 away from the 400.
questions.onCorrect: 50 N. The smaller pull cancels part of the larger one, and what is left over decides the direction.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two pulls. They are in opposite directions, so one cancels part of the other.

questions.prompt: A crate has forces of 25 N right and 10 N left on it. With right positive, find the net force in newtons.
hints: Which force gets the minus sign?
Rightward forces are positive, leftward forces negative.
Add the two signed forces.
questions.onCorrect: +15 N. A leftward force counts as negative, so it takes away from the rightward one.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes. The forces point opposite ways.
The size is right, but the larger force points right. The net force is positive.

questions.prompt: Why do both leftward forces get a minus sign?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: They point opposite to the direction chosen as positive.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They point opposite to the direction chosen as positive.

choices.label: They point opposite to the direction chosen as positive.
They are smaller than the rightward force.

questions.onCorrect: The sign records direction, not size. Anything pointing against the positive direction is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not set the sign. Direction does.
A leftward force can be as strong as a rightward one. The sign only records direction.

questions.prompt: A rope pulls a block right with 50 N. A second rope pulls it left. The block moves right at a constant velocity. How big is the leftward pull, in newtons?
hints: What does constant velocity say about the net force?
The two pulls must cancel.
How big must the second pull be to cancel the first?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Constant velocity means zero net force, so the leftward pull is also 50 N.

questions.onCorrect: 50 N. Constant velocity means zero net force, so the pulls are equal and opposite.

misconceptions.feedback: With no leftward pull, the block would speed up. Constant velocity needs the two to cancel.
Together they would give 100 N of pull in total, but the net force must be zero.
